item.title: Memory Bandwidth
item.description: Between the CPU registers and RAM lies a hierarchy of caches. Levels nearer a core are usually smaller and quicker; levels farther away are larger and slower. Two different quantities are hidden inside the word “quick”: latency is the delay between issuing a request and receiving the value; bandwidth is the amount of data the system can transfer per unit of time once enough requests are in flight. Bandwidth is often the binding resource for loops that perform little work per element.

item.title: Memory Latency
item.description: Bandwidth is easiest to expose with many independent requests: the out-of-order core, prefetchers, and memory subsystem can overlap them. Measuring latency requires the opposite experiment—each address must depend on the value returned by the previous load. A standard construction is one randomly ordered cycle. Every node is visited exactly once per lap, but the next address cannot be known until the current node arrives: std::vector<std::uint32_t> order(N), next(N); std::iota(order.begin(), order.end(), 0); std::mt19937 rng(42); std::shuffle(order.

item.title: Cache Lines
item.description: CPU caches transfer and track fixed-size blocks called cache lines. A 64-byte line is common on current x86-64 and AArch64 systems, but it is not universal; query the target machine rather than baking the number into a portable interface. When a load misses, the hierarchy normally fetches the entire line containing the requested byte. An ordinary store miss in write-back memory normally obtains ownership of the line first, as discussed in Memory Bandwidth.

item.title: Memory Sharing
item.description: Some levels of the memory hierarchy are shared. Sharing saves die area and lets one idle core leave more capacity to another, but it also creates contention for cache space, request queues, interconnect links, and DRAM bandwidth. The boundary is architecture-specific. Separate cores commonly have private L1 caches, but simultaneous hardware threads may share them; some processors share L2 within a cluster; and a last-level cache may be partitioned into slices rather than acting as one uniform pool.

item.title: Memory-Level Parallelism
item.description: A core can have several cache misses in flight at once. This overlap is called memory-level parallelism (MLP). It is why a linear scan can approach bandwidth, while one dependent pointer-chasing chain pays almost the full latency of every miss. MLP counts outstanding misses, not arbitrary loads and stores. A hundred loads that all hit L1 are not a hundred concurrent memory misses, and two requests can be in flight without the DRAM chips literally servicing them at the same instant.

item.title: Prefetching
item.description: If a future address is known early, the memory system can start fetching its line before the program needs the value. This prefetching converts latency into an overlapped request and consumes some of the memory-level parallelism available in the machine. Ordinary out-of-order execution already does this for independent loads in the instruction window. Two additional mechanisms reach farther: hardware prefetchers recognize address patterns in the stream of cache misses; software prefetch instructions give the processor a hint about a particular future address.

item.title: Alignment and Packing
item.description: An object is aligned when its address is a multiple of the alignment required by its type. The C++ requirement is alignof(T), not sizeof(T): the two often happen to be equal for small scalar types, but they are different properties. Alignment matters for correctness and performance. Some instructions require aligned operands. Even where unaligned loads are legal, an access that crosses a cache-line or page boundary may need two transfers and extra work to combine them.

item.title: Pointer Alternatives
Cache Associativity
item.description: Consider two versions of the strided increment over $N=2^{21}$ integers. One advances by 256 elements and the other by 257: for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; i += 256) ++a[i]; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; i += 257) ++a[i]; Their iteration counts differ by less than half a percent, yet the second loop was about ten times faster in the historical Zen 2 experiment. item.title: Memory Paging
item.description: Return once more to the strided increment, but keep the number of useful updates fixed at $N=2^{13}$ while growing the allocation with the stride $D$: constexpr std::size_t N = 1u << 13; std::vector<std::uint32_t> a(D * N, 0); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); i += D) ++a[i]; The production benchmark checks that D * N does not overflow, allocates on the heap, and consumes a checksum. For $D \ge 16$, successive accesses are at least one 64-byte line apart, so there are $N$ useful accesses and approximately $N$ touched data lines.

item.title: AoS and SoA
item.description: Data used together should usually be stored together. This improves spatial locality: one fetched line supplies several useful fields, adjacent lines are friendly to prefetchers, and translations cover more work. The familiar choice is between: an array of structures (AoS), where all fields of one record are consecutive; a structure of arrays (SoA), where each field forms its own consecutive stream. Neither layout is universally better. AoS favors operations that consume most fields of one record.
